actions.justification: Mandatory first step to establish baseline vital signs in this patient presenting with severe headache, blurred vision, and markedly elevated MAP of 160 mmHg consistent with hypertensive emergency.
Mandatory action to accurately characterize blood pressure in both arms (especially critical given history of aortic dissection) and confirm hypertensive emergency.

Mandatory assessment to identify end-organ damage (neurological, cardiac, renal) given severe headache, blurred vision, elevated MAP, and history of aortic dissection — findings will guide urgency and choice of antihypertensive therapy.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with a MAP of 160 mmHg, suggesting hypertensive emergency. Neurological assessment is critical to evaluate for hypertensive encephalopathy, intracranial hemorrhage, or other end-organ damage, especially given comorbid aortic dissection. This aligns with guideline requirements for neurological evaluation in this context.

Continuous blood pressure monitoring is essential in this hypertensive emergency to track BP trends, guide antihypertensive therapy titration, and detect rapid changes. Patient has MAP of 160 and comorbid aortic dissection, making real-time BP monitoring critical for safety.

Given the combination of severe headache, blurred vision, significantly elevated MAP (160 mmHg), and comorbid aortic dissection, neurology consultation is warranted to assist in evaluating for hypertensive emergency complications such as hypertensive encephalopathy or intracranial hemorrhage.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision — CT head is urgently needed to rule out hemorrhagic stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy, or intracranial pathology before initiating aggressive antihypertensive therapy.
Patient has known aortic dissection as a comorbidity. Chest X-ray is essential to evaluate for mediastinal widening or other signs of aortic pathology contributing to the hypertensive emergency.

Hypertensive emergency with MAP 160 and known aortic dissection requires urgent BP reduction. IV labetalol is the preferred agent in aortic dissection as it reduces both heart rate and BP, decreasing aortic wall stress. Initiate after imaging to confirm no contraindications.

BMP is essential to assess end-organ damage from hypertensive emergency, including renal function (creatinine, BUN), electrolytes, and glucose. Patient has hypertension and aortic dissection as comorbidities — renal involvement must be evaluated.

ECG is indicated to evaluate for cardiac involvement in hypertensive emergency, including signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, ischemia, or strain pattern. Also important given aortic dissection history.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with markedly elevated MAP (160 mmHg), raising concern for hypertensive encephalopathy or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). MRI brain provides better assessment of white matter changes than CT, which has already been completed.
CBC to assess for hematologic abnormalities, infection, or thrombocytopenia that may complicate hypertensive emergency management in a patient with known aortic dissection.
Coagulation studies are critical in a patient with aortic dissection and hypertensive emergency to assess bleeding risk and guide anticoagulation decisions.
eGFR to assess renal end-organ damage from hypertensive emergency; important for medication dosing and nephrology consult decision in context of markedly elevated MAP.
Urinalysis is essential to assess for renal end-organ damage (proteinuria, hematuria, casts) in hypertensive emergency, which guides severity classification and management.

Troponin should be obtained to evaluate for cardiac end-organ damage (hypertensive emergency can cause demand ischemia or type 2 MI), especially important given the known aortic dissection comorbidity.
Continuous urine output monitoring is indicated in hypertensive emergency to detect acute kidney injury as a sign of ongoing end-organ damage and to guide fluid management.

Patient with hypertensive emergency and aortic dissection comorbidity with neurological symptoms (severe headache, blurred vision) requires ICU-level monitoring for continuous BP management and end-organ surveillance.
